papers.title: Crystal and Dislocation Characteristics of Ti-6Al-4V Alloy Under Effect of Laser Shock Peening
papers.abstract: Laser shock peening (LSP) is an effective method for enhancing the fatigue life and mechanical properties of Ti alloys. However, there is limited research on the effects of LSP on crystal structure and dislocation characteristics. In this study, Ti-6Al-4V alloy was subjected to laser shock peening with varying laser power levels. The influence of laser power on the microstructure of Ti-6Al-4V was investigated, with a focus on the evolution of the cross-sectional structure, crystallographic features, and dislocation behavior. These characteristics were analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Following laser shock peening, the surface grains of Ti-6Al-4V alloy exhibited a distinct preferred orientation and underwent significant refinement, resulting in the formation of nanocrystals. At a laser power of 8 J, the texture strength decreased to 5.19 mud. As laser power increased, a denser dislocation structure and high-density dislocation regions formed at the surface, and the subgrain size further decreased, reaching 66 nm at 8 J. These findings provide valuable insights into grain refinement and property enhancement, contributing to the understanding of process-microstructure-property relationships.

papers.title: Henry Philip Wynn, 1945–2024
papers.abstract: Henry was born in Barnsley on 19 February 1945 and died on 2 November 2024. He was soon thrust into the world of statistics as his father, Arthur Wynn, was shortly to become Director of the Safety in Mines Research Establishment, where he worked on mining accident data with Egon Pearson, and the two families became close. Later, by coincidence, the Wynn family moved into a house in Highgate, which had been occupied by the sister of Karl Pearson. Egon had visited the house as a youngster and his childhood graffiti was found there. Henry’s mother Margaret Wynn, was the equally distinguished writer on social policy and he never really deviated from the strong support for the social democratic tradition his parents inspired. After the family moved to London from Sheffield, Henry was educated at Westminster School, gained his BA Honors in Mathematics at Oxford and a PhD in Mathematical Statistics at Imperial College London. At Oxford, he was a student at the new Jacobsen-designed campus of St Catherine’s College, in only its second year. He considered himself fortunate to have had Graham Segal as his pure mathematics tutor with Alan Taylor and John Ockendon for applied mathematics. At Imperial, his PhD supervisor was David Cox, and Agnes Herzberg was also a strong influence. Henry was involved in most of the major advances in experimental design, stemming from the work of Jack Kiefer, Jacob Wolfowitz, and coresearchers. His first major result was the algorithm for constructing D-optimum experimental designs, known today as the Wynn–Fedorov algorithm. It was for this work that he received the RSS Guy Medal in Silver in 1982. Both Kiefer and Fedorov visited Imperial College early in the 1970s. Later, in joint work with Kiefer, he was one of the first to study optimal design for correlated observations, and helped edit the experimental design volume of Kiefer’s collected works. He was a member of Jerome (Jerry) Sacks’ team, which wrote the highly sighted paper on computer experiments in 1989, which led to many theoretical developments and wide applications from engineering design to climate modeling. Henry was on the committee for the 6-month workshop on Uncertainty Quantification at the Isaac Newton Institute in 2018, in which these developments are well represented. Kiefer and Sacks were strong intellectual influences throughout his working life. Two other research areas grew out of this, the now much quoted work with Michael Shewry on Maximum Entropy Sampling and with Eva Riccomagno and others on low discrepancy sequences for Fourier regression. On the more classical optimal design Henry and Alessandra (Sandra) Giovagnoli developed Group-Majorization using its application to matrix majorization. The work on information and design was extended with Paula Sebastiani and with Werner Müller and Markus Hainy. Further, work with Alessandra (Sandra) Giovagnoli led to a new multivariate ‘dispersion ordering’. Henry completed postdoctoral research with David Bartholomew in 1970–1972, in the area of Markov Chain modeling in manpower studies. After one year as a Statistician in the Government Statistical Service, he returned to Imperial College as a Lecturer in 1972. Two events then occurred, which had a considerable effect on Henry’s international exposure. The first was a very formative year at the University of California, Berkeley 1975/6 and the second in 1977 was a challenge to the RSS Council’s nomination of Sir Campbell Adamson as a candidate for President. Previous Presidents had always been nominated and returned unopposed. However, with the requisite signatures for his nomination from (now) well-known individuals, Henry went to win the first election for President by a 3:2 majority. He then completed a successful 1-year presidency introducing some mild reforms and by all reports enjoying himself immensely. There has not been a contested election since. It should be understood that this took place toward the end of a period of radicalization of students, which started in the late 1960s. Indeed, Henry led a delegation to support the Paris students who participated in civil unrest in 1968 and was always proud of being a ‘soixanthuitard’. His radicalism never left him and was evident in his presidential address on the Freedom of Statistical Information in 1978, a topic that is still very relevant today. An early paper on multiple comparisons with Peter Bloomfield when they were both PhD students at Imperial College, and further work with Robert Bohrer and his then student Dan Naiman led to two seminal papers with Naiman on tight inclusions-exclusion relations using ideas from geometry and topology. It is now realized that these constructions are precisely those now used in the foundation of topological data analysis. Naiman and Wynn called them ‘discrete tubes’ after the work of Robert Adler and Rips or alpha-complexes is now more common. Naiman and Wynn’s realization of the close connection between these constructions and minimal free resolutions in topology enabled an application, via monomial ideals, to reliability theory, first with Beatrice Giglio and then with Eduardo Sáenz-de-Cabezón and later also with Fatemeh Mohammadi in a long series of papers. Although using reflection groups (as in the earlier joint work with Giovagnoli) rather than monomial ideals after a chance meeting at Statistical and Applied Mathematical Sciences Institute (SAMSI) in North Carolina, Henry started active research with Andrew Francis, notably the application of the theory of ‘buildings’ to nonparametric statistics. Henry took up the Chair in Mathematical Statistics at City University in 1985, becoming Dean of Mathematics 2 years later and the founding codirector of the Engineering Design Centre. This was a period in which he was intimately involved in the introduction of Robust Engineering Design into Europe, following on from Jerry Sacks’ series of National Science Foundation workshops in the USA, the Sacks et al. paper, and the rapid resurgence of interests in quality improvement, in the USA and UK via a series of EU grants Henry worked with major companies in Europe, notably Fiat and Volvo. This was one of the influences, which led to the launch of the European Network of Business and Industrial Statistics (ENBIS), of which he was the founding President and he was later awarded its Box Medal. Much of this work continued when he was appointed Professor of Industrial Statistics and founding Director of the Risk Initiative and Statistical Consultancy Unit (RISCU) at the University of Warwick in 1995, with more UK and European grants shifting more into the environmental modeling area notably with the Swedish Environmental Research Institute (IVL). RISCU became a leading UK group, with many industrial projects. Throughout this period Ronald Bates, from City University, Warwick and LSE, and who eventually took a senior position in Rolls Royce, was Henry’s closest Research Fellow. Henry was a founder Committee Member on the series of Model-oriented Data Analysis (MODA) conferences on Optimal Design. Valerii V. Fedorov and Anthony Atkinson (a colleague at Imperial College) were also members as were Luc Pronzato and Anatoly Zhigljavski, who then became close collaborators leading to an opus of over 20 joint papers. The novel idea in their first work was that some search and optimization algorithms, similar in style to the original Wynn–Fedorov algorithm, could be turned into dynamical systems via a normalization step so that the rate of convergence could be measured by the Kolmogorov–Shannon entropy of the system. They studied the steepest descent algorithm in detail and were able to improve on Kiefer’s Golden-section Fibonacci search in the GS4 algorithm, consolidated in a monograph in 1998. They continued to work together on topics related to dispersion and information. Pronzato and Zhigljavski edited Henry’s 60th birthday Festschrift volume, which is a good compendium of their joint and related work up to 2009. Following a key joint paper with Giovanni Pistone and the application of Gröbner Basis theory to the aliasing problem in experimental design, Henry and Giovanni joined forces with Eva Riccomagno to write a monograph on ‘Algebraic Statistics’ and ran a series of successful workshops called GROSTAT. The subject had already been initiated by the seminal work of Persi Diaconis and Berndt Sturmfels. Henry’s work on reliability comes under the same heading, as does continued joint work on design with Eva Riccomagno and Hugo Maruri and others, and a well-cited paper on differential algebra in SIR modeling of epidemics. Henry was appointed Professor and Head of the Department of Statistics at the London School of Economics in 2003 and continued active research in all his main areas right up until and beyond retirement. Notable was his participation in the large multicenter project MUCM on computer experiments led by Anthony O’Hagan and the even larger project CELSIUS on district heating in Europe, led partly by his previous contacts with IVL in Sweden. Henry’s move to LSE added more decision-oriented material, and his early radicalism reemerged. He was a leader of a campaign to abolish the retirement age for academics complete with website and blog and offered assistance to other academics. The eventual change in the law was just too late for him to benefit, although he remained at LSE as Emeritus Professor and part-time Professorial Research Fellow and later held a part-time research post at the Alan Turing Institute. Of his many outside activities, he was probably most proud of being the codirector of the Eindhoven based stochastics center EURANDOM from 2000 to 2005 and the Chair of the Advisory Committee of Oslo-based Statistics For Industry Centre (SFI) from 2005 to 2010. Henry had been a Fellow of the RSS since 1969. He served on the RSS Research Section Committee several times between 1973 and 1998. Henry was still an active member of the Society until very recently, having joined the inaugural honors search committee in 2023 to award the latest Guy Medals and his enthusiasm made a tremendous impact. Henry leaves two sons, Hamish and Robin, by his first wife, Sandra, and was happily married for over 30 years to his second wife, the distinguished photographer Jan Baldwin.
